segments.text: In this episode of the UX Tea Break, I talk about a foolproof method for writing good
survey questions.
I was asked this question in a training class by Grace Hall. Grace said, "My boss has asked me to do
a survey with our customers. Any tips on writing good survey questions?"
So, I chose this question because I’ve not been very complementary about surveys in the past.
In other videos, I’ve said most researchers would be better off running a field visit
or a usability test rather than a survey. I stand by that but that doesn’t mean I’m
anti-survey. Done well, a survey can provide great insights. The problem is that surveys
aren’t often done well. One of the biggest culprits is having poorly phrased survey questions.
Everyone thinks they are good at asking questions but the fact is that creating good survey
questions is hard. Even a simple question like, "Do you know the time?" can be answered
in different ways. You might answer, “It’s 10am”. But you could also answer, "It’s
tea time" (let’s be honest, it’s always tea time). Or you could just answer "Yes,
I know the time". The point is, different people interpret the question in different
ways.
Now, experienced survey practitioners are aware of these issues and have an incredibly
useful tool you can use to test your own survey questions. It's called the cognitive interview.
The cognitive interview is a technique for pilot testing questions on surveys. The way
it works is you ask a volunteer the question on your survey — but you're not really interested
in their answer. With a cognitive interview, you’re more interested in how your participants
arrived at their answer. In some ways, a cognitive interview is similar to a usability test:
you ask a participant to "think aloud" as they try to answer the question.
Here’s how to do it. You ask your volunteer your survey question, and you show them the
response categories you’ve provided. Then you wait for the answer. Once the participant’s
answered, you then ask these questions, one by one:
First, you ask: “In your own words, what is this question asking?"
Then, you ask: "How did you arrive at your answer?"
And finally, you ask: "How sure are you of your answer?"
Let's take a topical question like, "How many times have you talked to a doctor in the last
year?" Imagine we ask our participant that question, and let’s say they choose the
option on our survey labelled "1-4". Remember, we’re not so much interested in the answer
as in how they arrived at their answer. So after our volunteer has answered, we first
ask: “In your own words, what is this question asking?”
This question helps us discover if the volunteer has interpreted the survey question in the
way we intended. Let me give you an example. When I pilot tested the "doctor" question
with a volunteer just now, I discovered a few problems. My volunteer wasn’t sure if
she should count visits to the Doctor's surgery when she saw the Practice Nurse, but not the
doctor. Or if she should count those times when she talked to the doctor about her child's
health, rather than her own.
Next we ask, "How did you arrive at your answer?" Taking our "doctor" question, appointments
can be easy to forget, particularly if they happened more than a few months ago. My volunteer
pointed out that it wasn’t clear if the question meant the last 12 months or the last
calendar year.
And lastly, we ask "How sure are you of your answer?” What we want to find out is how
our volunteer made their estimate. As another example, imagine I asked you a question like,
"In the past month, how many times have you brushed your teeth?”. The chances are, you
would probably resort to an average ("I do it twice a day, so…"). But this can risk
an overestimation because you forget the times you went to bed drunk or tired or skipped
brushing your teeth for some other reason. Another issue here is that people may edit
their responses to be socially desirable. So with our doctor question, imagine we offer
choices like "0", "1-4", "5-10" and "More than 11". If you’ve been to the doctor 5
times, you may decide to pick "1-4" so as not appear like a hypochondriac.
So the best way to design good survey questions — like the best way to design anything — is
to test it. In this case, with a cognitive interview. Then you iterate, and test again.
I hope you found this useful. If you have a question you’d like me to answer, write
it in the comments below.
